nodes.title: SQL Server query tuning
nodes.tease: Same query, same data, 2 seconds for one user and 40 for the next. What did SQL Server remember?

primer.problem: A report or screen that was fast last month now times out, and users blame 'the database'. Tuning means finding out why SQL Server chose a slow way to fetch the rows, then giving it a better option: a better index, a rewritten predicate, fresher statistics or a different plan.
primer.picture: Think of the optimizer as a route planner. It reads **statistics** (a map of how many rows each value has), estimates the cost of each route and caches the winning **execution plan**. A **clustered index** is the table itself sorted by its key; a **nonclustered index** is a separate sorted list pointing back to it. If the plan's estimated rows are far from the actual rows, the map was wrong, and the route is probably wrong too.
primer.sketch:
query + parameters
      │
      ▼
 optimizer ── reads ──▶ statistics (histogram)
      │
      ▼
 cached plan:  Index Seek ─▶ Key Lookup ─▶ Nested Loops
      │
      ▼
 compare estimated rows vs actual rows

terms.def: The tree of physical operators (seek, scan, join, sort) SQL Server picked to run a query, with estimated and actual row counts.
A nonclustered index holding every column a query needs, via key or INCLUDE columns, so no lookup to the base table happens.
Search ARGument-able: a predicate written so the engine can seek an index range instead of evaluating every row.
SQL Server compiles a cached plan using the first parameter values it sees, then reuses that plan for every later value.
Per-column histograms of up to 200 steps that the optimizer uses to estimate how many rows a predicate returns.
An extra trip from a nonclustered index into the clustered index to fetch columns the index does not contain.

inPractice.setting: A grocery chain's order back office: 900 stores, 60 million order rows in SQL Server 2022
inPractice.story:
The store-replenishment screen at a 900-store grocery chain loaded in under a second for years. Then, on the Monday after a quarterly data load, it took 40 seconds and the buying team declared the database broken. Nobody had deployed code.

The DBA started where the lesson says: the **actual execution plan** plus `SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON`. The plan estimated 12 rows from `dbo.Orders` and got 310,000. The weekend load had added 8 million rows, and auto-update had not fired yet, so the histogram still described last quarter. `UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.Orders WITH FULLSCAN` brought the screen back to 1.1 seconds before lunch.

Two weeks later the same procedure crawled again, but only for the biggest distribution centre. Query Store showed the cause: a plan compiled for a tiny store, nested loops plus a **key lookup** per row, reused for a store with 50,000 order lines. That was **parameter sniffing**. The team moved the database to compatibility level 160 so Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization could cache separate variants, and forced the known-good plan in Query Store as a safety net.

While in there they fixed the predicate too: `WHERE CAST(OrderDate AS date) = @day` became a **SARGable** range, and a covering index `(StoreId, OrderDate) INCLUDE (Qty, Sku)` removed the lookups. Logical reads dropped from 1.4 million to 3,200, and stats updates are now a step at the end of every bulk load.
inPractice.flow:
replenishment screen --@storeId,@day--> usp_GetStoreOrders
   optimizer --reads--> stats on dbo.Orders (stale after bulk load)
   cached plan: Index Seek -> Key Lookup x50k -> Nested Loops  (slow)
fix: UPDATE STATISTICS + compat 160 (PSP) + forced plan in Query Store
   new plan: Index Seek on IX_Orders_Store_Date (covering) -> done
inPractice.takeaway: When a query suddenly slows, I compare estimated and actual rows in the plan first; stale statistics and parameter sniffing explain most cases before any index changes.

lesson.body:
Start every diagnosis with the **actual execution plan** plus `SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON`. Logical reads tell you how much work was done; the gap between **estimated and actual rows** tells you whether the optimizer was misinformed. Query Store shows whether the plan changed and when.

A table has one **clustered index**: the leaf level is the data, ordered by the key, so pick a narrow, ever-increasing, unique key. **Nonclustered indexes** store their key plus the clustered key as a row locator. When a seek finds rows but the query needs other columns, each row costs a **key lookup**; at a few rows that is fine, at 50,000 rows the optimizer flips to a scan. Adding the missing columns with `INCLUDE` makes the index **covering**.

An index only helps if the predicate is **SARGable**. `WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024`, `WHERE LEFT(Code,3) = 'ABC'` or comparing a varchar column to an nvarchar parameter wraps the column in a function or implicit conversion, so SQL Server cannot seek. Rewrite as a range on the bare column: `OrderDate >= '2024-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-01-01'`.

**Parameter sniffing**: a stored procedure compiled for a tiny customer caches a nested-loops plan; the next call for the biggest customer reuses it and crawls. Options: `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` for infrequent report queries, `OPTIMIZE FOR`, forcing a known-good plan in Query Store, or SQL Server 2022's Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization (compatibility level 160), which caches several plan variants.

**Statistics** go stale after big loads; auto-update triggers on a modification threshold that may not have fired yet. After a bulk load, `UPDATE STATISTICS` on the affected tables is often the whole fix.

source.title: SQL Server and Azure SQL index architecture and design guide

cards.prompt: An actual plan shows an Index Seek estimating 12 rows that returns 480,000, feeding a Nested Loops join. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Stale statistics or a sniffed parameter gave the optimizer a wrong row estimate
The clustered index is fragmented
The server needs more CPU cores
Nested Loops joins are always slower than Hash joins
cards.why: A huge estimated-vs-actual gap means the optimizer was misinformed, so it chose a plan suited to 12 rows. Fragmentation affects scan I/O a little but does not explain a 40,000x estimation error.

cards.prompt: Which predicate lets SQL Server seek an index on OrderDate?
options: OrderDate >= '20240101' AND OrderDate < '20250101'
YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024
CONVERT(date, OrderDate) BETWEEN ... with OrderDate wrapped in DATEADD
FORMAT(OrderDate, 'yyyy') = '2024'
cards.why: A range on the bare column is SARGable. Wrapping the column in YEAR, DATEADD or FORMAT hides it from the index, forcing a scan that evaluates every row.

cards.prompt: A table can have several clustered indexes as long as their keys differ.
cards.why: The clustered index is the table's data ordered by its key, so there can only be one. You can have up to 999 nonclustered indexes, each pointing back to it.

cards.prompt: Adding non-key columns to a nonclustered index with the ___ clause makes it covering and removes key lookups.
cards.why: INCLUDE columns live only in the leaf level, so they widen the index less than adding them to the key and do not affect sort order, yet the query no longer needs the base table.

cards.prompt: A report proc is fast for most customers but slow for the largest one, and fast again after the plan cache is cleared. Which fix is the most targeted?
options: Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the statement or force a good plan via Query Store
Rebuild every index nightly
Switch the database to SIMPLE recovery
Add NOLOCK hints to the query
cards.why: That pattern is parameter sniffing: the cached plan suits whoever compiled it first. Rebuilding indexes 'fixes' it only by accident, because it invalidates plans; NOLOCK changes isolation, not plan choice.

cards.prompt: SQL Server 2022 added ___ optimization, which caches multiple plans for one parameterized query depending on parameter values.
cards.why: PSP optimization (compatibility level 160) buckets parameter values by cardinality and keeps a plan variant per bucket, the engine's built-in answer to classic parameter sniffing.

explain.prompt: Your CV says you did performance tuning on SQL Server. Pick one slow query you fixed and walk me through how you found the cause.
explain.modelAnswer: Frame it with your own case: which screen or report, how slow, who complained. Then the method. First I reproduced it with the real parameters and captured the actual execution plan with SET STATISTICS IO and TIME on, so I had logical reads and elapsed time as a baseline. I looked for the operator with the most reads and for the biggest gap between estimated and actual rows. In my case [name it: a scan caused by a function on a date column / a key lookup repeated thousands of times / a sniffed plan]. The fix was [rewrite the predicate as a range / add a covering index with INCLUDE columns / OPTION RECOMPILE or a Query Store forced plan / update statistics after the load]. I verified by comparing reads and duration before and after with the same parameters, and checked the new index did not hurt writes on that table. The habit I took away: measure first, change one thing, measure again, and never guess from the query text alone.
rubric: Reproduces with real parameters before changing anything
Uses the actual plan and STATISTICS IO/TIME as evidence
Names a concrete root cause (SARGability, lookup, sniffing, stats)
Fix matches the cause, not a generic 'added an index'
Verifies with before/after numbers and considers write cost

scenarios.situation: The ERP's payroll summary screen jumped from 1 second to 25 seconds the morning after a month-end import added 2 million rows. No code was deployed. The HR lead needs payroll approved by noon.
scenarios.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Capture the actual plan, compare estimated and actual rows, and if estimates are off update statistics on the imported tables, then re-test
options.why: A large load with no code change points at stale statistics or a plan compiled for the old data. Evidence first, and the fix is fast and low risk before the deadline.

options.text: Add the missing index that the plan's green hint suggests
options.why: Sometimes right, but missing-index hints ignore existing indexes and write cost; doing it before checking estimates may mask the real stale-statistics cause.

options.text: Add WITH (NOLOCK) to every table in the query
options.why: NOLOCK does not change the plan shape and introduces dirty and duplicate reads into a payroll figure, which is the last place you want them.

nodes.title: Raw SQL for reports
nodes.tease: Your report cursors over 80,000 rows. One window function does it in a single pass. Which?

primer.problem: Business reports need rankings, running totals, month-over-month changes and 'latest row per employee'. Written row by row they are slow and they lock tables that the live app is writing to. The skill is expressing them as one set-based query that reads consistently without blocking users.
primer.picture: Think of LINQ versus a foreach loop: you describe the whole set and the engine picks how. **CTEs** are named subqueries that make a long report readable top to bottom. **Window functions** compute per-row values over a group of rows (the window) without collapsing them like GROUP BY does. **Isolation levels** decide what a reader sees while writers are busy; **RCSI** lets readers see the last committed version instead of waiting on locks.

terms.def: Common Table Expression: a named, query-scoped result set introduced with WITH, readable like a variable, optionally recursive.
A function with an OVER clause that computes a value per row from a set of related rows, keeping every row.
The part of OVER that splits rows into independent groups; the function restarts for each group.
Read Committed Snapshot Isolation: readers get the last committed row version instead of waiting on writers' locks.
Two sessions each hold a lock the other needs; SQL Server kills one as victim with error 1205.

inPractice.setting: A hospital group's staffing team reporting nurse overtime across 14 hospitals
inPractice.story:
The nurse-overtime report at a 14-hospital group was a stored procedure with a cursor over 120,000 shift rows. For each nurse it read every shift, added hours into a variable and wrote a row to a results table. It took 11 minutes, and while it ran the rostering app, which writes shifts all day, kept timing out on blocked updates.

A developer rewrote it as a chain of **CTEs**: filter the pay period, aggregate hours per nurse per week, then compute. `SUM(Hours) OVER (PARTITION BY NurseId ORDER BY WeekStart ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` gave the running total, and `LAG` gave week-over-week change. She specified `ROWS` deliberately, since the default `RANGE` frame would have used the slower on-disk spool. Latest contract per nurse came from **ROW_NUMBER** with `rn = 1`. The report dropped to 6 seconds.

The blocking did not fully go away. Under default READ COMMITTED the report still took shared locks, and one night a rostering update and the report hit each other in opposite order and SQL Server killed the report with error 1205. The `xml_deadlock_report` in `system_health` showed both statements. The team enabled **READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT**, so the report reads the last committed versions and no longer blocks writers, and added a retry on 1205 in the app layer. Someone suggested `NOLOCK` instead; it was rejected because it can double-count rows during page splits, which in an overtime report means paying someone twice.
inPractice.flow:
dbo.Shifts (rostering app writes all day)
   -> CTE period   (WHERE ShiftDate in pay period)
   -> CTE weekly   (GROUP BY NurseId, WeekStart)
   -> CTE ranked   (SUM OVER ROWS UNBOUNDED, LAG, ROW_NUMBER)
   -> SELECT ... WHERE rn = 1
reads under RCSI: last committed version, no shared locks on writers
inPractice.takeaway: I replace cursors with CTEs and window functions, and I fix report-versus-app blocking with RCSI rather than NOLOCK, which can return wrong numbers.

lesson.body:
A report query reads best as a pipeline of **CTEs**: filter the period, aggregate, rank, then present. A CTE is not materialised in SQL Server; the optimizer inlines it, so referencing the same CTE twice runs it twice. If you need it reused, use a temp table.

**Window functions** replace most cursors. `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY ValidFrom DESC)` then `WHERE rn = 1` gives the latest row per employee and is the standard dedupe. `SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY PayMonth ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` is a running total. Specify `ROWS`: with ORDER BY and no frame the default is `RANGE`, which treats ties as one and uses a slower on-disk spool. `LAG(Amount) OVER (... ORDER BY PayMonth)` reads the previous row, so month-over-month change is one expression. Window functions cannot appear in WHERE, which is why you wrap them in a CTE first.

**Set-based versus cursor**: a cursor does one seek and one write per row with per-statement overhead; the set-based version lets the engine pick a single scan, hash or merge. Cursors are only justified for genuinely sequential logic like calling a proc per row.

**Locking**: the default READ COMMITTED takes shared locks, so a long report can block and be blocked by app writes. With **READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON** readers see the last committed version from the version store and do not block writers; it is the default in Azure SQL Database. `NOLOCK` is not the same: it reads uncommitted data and can skip or double-count rows during page splits.

**Deadlocks** are captured in the `system_health` Extended Events session (`xml_deadlock_report`). Fixes: access tables in the same order, keep transactions short, add indexes so fewer rows get locked, and retry on error 1205.
lesson.snippet:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT EmployeeId, PayMonth, SUM(Gross) AS Gross
  FROM dbo.Payslips
  WHERE PayMonth >= '20250101'
  GROUP BY EmployeeId, PayMonth
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
    LAG(Gross) OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY PayMonth) AS PrevGross,
    SUM(Gross) OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY PayMonth
                     ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS YtdGross,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY PayMonth DESC) AS rn
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT EmployeeId, PayMonth, Gross, Gross - PrevGross AS Delta, YtdGross
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;  -- latest month per employee

cards.prompt: You need the most recent contract row per employee from a history table. Which approach is standard?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY ValidFrom DESC), then filter rn = 1 in an outer query
GROUP BY EmployeeId with MAX(ValidFrom) and every other column in the SELECT
A cursor that keeps the last row it saw per employee
RANK() in the WHERE clause directly
cards.why: ROW_NUMBER picks exactly one row per partition and the outer filter keeps it. GROUP BY with MAX gives the date but not the other columns of that row, and window functions are not allowed in WHERE.

cards.prompt: To compare each month's total with the previous month's in one pass, use the window function ___.
cards.why: LAG reads a value from an earlier row in the same partition and order, so month-over-month delta needs no self-join. LEAD looks forward instead.

cards.prompt: In SQL Server, a CTE referenced twice in the same query is computed once and cached.
cards.why: SQL Server inlines CTEs like views, so each reference is evaluated separately. If the intermediate result is expensive and reused, materialise it in a temp table.

cards.prompt: A long report query is blocking the ERP's save operations. Which change stops readers and writers blocking each other while still reading only committed data?
options: Enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT on the database
Add WITH (NOLOCK) to the report
Switch the report to SERIALIZABLE
Wrap the report in BEGIN TRAN ... COMMIT
cards.why: RCSI serves readers the last committed row version, so they take no shared locks. NOLOCK also avoids blocking but reads uncommitted and can miss or double-count rows, which is wrong for figures someone signs off.

cards.prompt: Why write ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING explicitly in a running-total SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)?
options: Without it the default frame is RANGE, which lumps tied ORDER BY values together and runs slower
Without it SQL Server returns an error
ROWS makes the sum include future rows
It is required for PARTITION BY to work
cards.why: With ORDER BY and no frame the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, so rows sharing a date get the same total and the engine uses an on-disk worktable. ROWS is per-row and uses a faster in-memory spool.

cards.prompt: When SQL Server detects a deadlock it chooses one session as the victim and rolls back its transaction with error 1205.
cards.why: The lock monitor picks the cheapest transaction to roll back (or the one with lower DEADLOCK_PRIORITY). Application code should catch 1205 and retry, and you analyse the graph from the system_health session.

explain.prompt: Your CV says 'extensive raw SQL for reports'. Why raw SQL instead of Entity Framework for those, and how did you keep reports from hurting the live system?
explain.modelAnswer: EF Core is great for transactional work: load an aggregate, change it, save. Reports are different: they aggregate many rows, rank, compute running totals and period deltas. LINQ can express some of that, but the generated SQL is hard to control and window functions with explicit frames are clumsy, so for reports I wrote SQL directly, usually as a chain of CTEs with ROW_NUMBER, SUM OVER and LAG, sometimes in stored procedures called from EF with FromSql or Dapper-style mapping. Give your example here: [the government or ERP report, its volume]. To protect the live system I kept everything set-based, made predicates SARGable and indexed for the report's filters, checked the plan with real parameters, and avoided long transactions. For blocking I would use READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT rather than NOLOCK, because NOLOCK can return rows twice or not at all, which is unacceptable for figures someone signs off. Heavy recurring reports can also run off a readable replica or a scheduled snapshot.
rubric: Clear reason: reports are set-based aggregations EF expresses poorly
Names window functions and CTEs concretely
Keeps it set-based, indexed and SARGable
Prefers RCSI over NOLOCK and says why
Mentions offloading heavy reports (replica, snapshot, scheduled)

scenarios.situation: A colleague's month-end payroll report uses a cursor over 80,000 payslips to compute year-to-date gross per employee. It takes 9 minutes and HR runs it several times while correcting data.
scenarios.question: How do you approach the rewrite?

options.text: Replace the cursor with one query using SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY EmployeeId ORDER BY PayMonth ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING), and diff the output against the old report before switching
options.why: Set-based with an explicit frame is one pass, and diffing against the old output proves the payroll numbers did not change, which matters more than speed.

options.text: Keep the cursor but make it FAST_FORWARD and add an index
options.why: It helps somewhat, but it keeps per-row overhead and leaves the core problem in place.

options.text: Move the calculation into C# by loading all payslips into memory
options.why: It ships 80,000 rows over the wire to do what the engine does natively, and creates a second source of truth for payroll logic.

nodes.title: SSRS reports
nodes.tease: SQL Server 2025 shipped without a new SSRS. So where do your RDL reports live now?

primer.problem: Government clients and finance teams want fixed-layout, printable reports: payslips, tender summaries, monthly statements, exported to PDF or Excel and emailed on a schedule. Building these by hand in a web app is slow; a report server renders them from a query and a layout file.
primer.picture: SSRS is like a Razor view engine that runs on its own server. An **RDL** file is the template (XML layout), a **dataset** is the query that feeds it, **parameters** are the inputs the user picks. The **report server** stores reports in its catalog database, renders them to HTML, PDF or Excel, and **subscriptions** run them on a schedule through SQL Server Agent and email the result. In 2026 its successor on-premises is **Power BI Report Server**.

terms.def: Report Definition Language: the XML file describing a report's data sources, datasets, parameters and layout.
A pixel-precise, page-oriented report designed for printing or PDF, the kind SSRS produces.
The query or stored procedure inside a report that returns the rows a table or chart displays.
A scheduled delivery that renders a report and sends it by email or to a file share.
Microsoft's on-premises report portal that hosts paginated RDL reports plus interactive Power BI reports.

inPractice.setting: A regional public-sector pensions office running 85 paginated reports on SSRS 2022
inPractice.story:
A regional pensions office sent 4,000 statements a month: monthly benefit letters, arrears summaries and audit extracts, all as **RDL** reports on SSRS 2022 with SQL Server Standard. Each report's **dataset** called a stored procedure, and cascading parameters let a clerk pick a district, then a pensioner.

The trouble started with a server migration. The reports deployed fine, the web portal worked, and nobody noticed for three days that no statements had gone out. The **subscriptions** existed in the `ReportServer` catalog, but on the new box the SQL Server Agent service was set to manual and was stopped. Every subscription schedule is an Agent job, so no Agent meant no deliveries. They started Agent, set it to automatic and added a monitor on job failures.

The next wish was a **data-driven subscription** that would read each pensioner's preferred format and email from a table. That is an Enterprise feature, and they were on Standard, so a small nightly job wrote one file per district to a share instead.

Then the director heard that SSRS was being discontinued and asked for a rewrite budget. The developer showed the facts: no new SSRS shipped with SQL Server 2025, SSRS 2022 is supported until January 2033, and **Power BI Report Server** hosts the same RDL files and comes with their SQL Server 2025 licence. `ExecutionLog3` showed 23 reports unused for a year, so they moved 62.
inPractice.flow:
clerk / schedule --params--> report server (web service)
   -> RDL dataset --> usp_BenefitStatement (SQL Server)
   -> render PDF
subscription schedule = SQL Server Agent job --> email / file share
ExecutionLog3 --> who ran what, how long --> retire unused reports
inPractice.takeaway: SSRS skills still transfer in 2026: the same RDL reports run on Power BI Report Server, and I check that SQL Server Agent runs before trusting subscriptions.

lesson.body:
An SSRS installation has a **report server** (web service plus web portal) and two databases: `ReportServer`, the catalog holding reports, data sources, schedules and security, and `ReportServerTempDB` for sessions and cached results. You author an `.rdl` in Report Builder or a Visual Studio Report Server Project and deploy it to a folder.

Inside the RDL, a **data source** holds the connection (shared ones are reused across reports), and each **dataset** is a query or stored procedure. Report **parameters** map to query parameters; a parameter's available values can come from another dataset, which is how cascading drop-downs work (pick a department, then an employee). Multi-value parameters arrive in SQL as a list for `IN (@Dept)`. Keep the logic in a stored procedure so it is tuned and versioned like any other SQL.

**Subscriptions** render on a schedule and deliver via email or file share; each schedule is a SQL Server Agent job, so no Agent, no subscriptions. **Data-driven subscriptions**, where recipients and parameters come from a query, are an Enterprise feature. For performance you can cache reports or keep **snapshots**; the `ExecutionLog3` view records who ran which report, with which parameters and how long it took, useful both for tuning and as an audit trail.

Where it stands in 2026: Microsoft released **no new SSRS with SQL Server 2025**. On-premises reporting is consolidated into **Power BI Report Server**, which hosts the same RDL paginated reports plus Power BI reports and is now included with paid SQL Server 2025 licences (Enterprise and Standard), no longer only Enterprise with Software Assurance. SSRS 2022 remains supported until January 2033. In the cloud, the equivalent is paginated reports in the Power BI service (Fabric). So your RDL skills transfer; the hosting product changed.

cards.prompt: What happened to SSRS with SQL Server 2025?
options: No new SSRS version shipped; on-premises reporting is consolidated into Power BI Report Server
SSRS 2025 shipped with a new React-based portal
SSRS was removed and RDL reports no longer run anywhere
SSRS became an Azure-only service
cards.why: Microsoft stopped releasing SSRS after 2022 and points customers to Power BI Report Server, which renders the same RDL paginated reports. RDL did not die; only the hosting product changed.

cards.prompt: SSRS subscriptions depend on SQL Server Agent, because each schedule is created as an Agent job.
cards.why: The report server creates Agent jobs for schedules. If Agent is stopped, or you use an edition without it like Express, subscriptions silently stop firing.

cards.prompt: A report layout, its datasets and parameters are stored in an XML file with the extension ___.
cards.why: RDL (Report Definition Language) is the portable artefact: the same file deploys to SSRS, Power BI Report Server or the Power BI service as a paginated report.

cards.prompt: How do you build cascading parameters (choose a department, then only its employees appear)?
options: Give the Employee parameter an available-values dataset that filters by @Department
Write JavaScript in the report portal
Use two separate reports linked by a URL
Use a data-driven subscription
cards.why: A parameter's available values can come from a dataset that itself takes an earlier parameter, so SSRS refreshes the list when the first value changes. Subscriptions are about delivery, not interactivity.

cards.prompt: Which SSRS catalog view tells you who ran which report, with which parameters and how long rendering took?
options: ExecutionLog3
sys.dm_exec_requests
ReportServerTempDB.Sessions
msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory
cards.why: ExecutionLog3 in the ReportServer database splits time into data retrieval, processing and rendering, so you know whether to tune the query or the layout. sysjobhistory only shows Agent job outcomes.

cards.prompt: With SQL Server 2025, Power BI Report Server is still limited to Enterprise edition customers with Software Assurance.
cards.why: Microsoft broadened access: paid SQL Server 2025 licences, including Standard, get Power BI Report Server. Previously it required Enterprise plus Software Assurance or Power BI Premium.

explain.prompt: You list SSRS reports. Describe how one of your reports was built end to end, and what you would use for the same need today.
explain.modelAnswer: Pick your real report: what it showed, for which client, how often. Structurally it was an RDL authored in Visual Studio or Report Builder, with a shared data source to SQL Server and a dataset calling a stored procedure, because I wanted the SQL tuned and versioned with the rest of the database. Parameters such as period and department mapped to proc parameters, with available values from small lookup datasets so the lists cascaded. The layout used a tablix with grouping for subtotals, and users exported to PDF or Excel. If it was scheduled, a subscription delivered it by email, which runs as a SQL Server Agent job. For slow renders, ExecutionLog3 shows whether time goes into data retrieval or rendering. Today: Microsoft shipped no new SSRS with SQL Server 2025, so on-premises I would host the same RDL on Power BI Report Server, which now comes with paid SQL Server licences; in the cloud, paginated reports in Power BI. The RDL and SQL skills carry over directly.
rubric: Describes data source, dataset (ideally a stored procedure) and parameters
Mentions layout/grouping and export formats
Knows subscriptions run via SQL Server Agent
Knows SSRS 2022 is the last release and PBIRS is the successor
Mentions a cloud option (Power BI paginated reports)

scenarios.situation: A government client running SSRS 2022 asks whether they must rewrite 120 RDL reports because 'SSRS is being discontinued'. They are planning a SQL Server 2025 upgrade next year on-premises.
scenarios.question: What do you advise?

options.text: Explain SSRS 2022 is supported until 2033, and that Power BI Report Server hosts the same RDL files; pilot a handful of reports on PBIRS before planning the migration
options.why: Accurate on support dates, avoids a needless rewrite, and a pilot surfaces the few incompatibilities before committing.

options.text: Stay on SSRS 2022 indefinitely and ignore the change
options.why: Safe until 2033, but leaves them without a plan and stuck on an end-of-line product.

options.text: Rewrite all reports as custom Angular pages with a PDF library
options.why: Large cost and risk to reproduce pixel-precise paginated output that the successor product already renders.

nodes.title: PostgreSQL vs SQL Server
nodes.tease: In Postgres an UPDATE never overwrites a row. So where does the old one go, and who cleans it up?

primer.problem: At Moveo some services ran on PostgreSQL next to SQL Server. Interviewers want to know you understand what actually differs underneath, not just syntax, and when you would pick each. For an AI role, PostgreSQL also matters because pgvector can hold RAG embeddings next to ordinary data.
primer.picture: SQL Server by default updates rows in place and uses locks so readers wait; turn on RCSI and it keeps old versions in a side store. PostgreSQL always works like that: every UPDATE writes a **new row version** in the table itself, and readers see whichever version their snapshot allows. The price is **dead tuples** that **VACUUM** must clean. Extensions bolt on features like plugins in .NET: **pgvector** adds a vector type and similarity indexes.
primer.sketch:
UPDATE salary = 5000
  table heap:  [v1 salary=4000 (dead)]  [v2 salary=5000 (live)]
                     │
  old snapshot still sees v1 until it ends
                     │
  VACUUM later marks v1's space reusable

terms.def: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: writers create new row versions so readers see a consistent snapshot without locking.
An old row version no transaction can still see, occupying space until VACUUM reclaims it.
PostgreSQL maintenance that marks dead tuples' space reusable and protects against transaction ID wraparound; autovacuum runs it automatically.
PostgreSQL's binary JSON column type, indexable with GIN and queryable with operators like @> for containment.
An open-source PostgreSQL extension adding a vector column type, distance operators and HNSW or IVFFlat indexes.

inPractice.setting: A legal-tech startup building clause search over 300,000 clauses on RDS PostgreSQL
inPractice.story:
A legal-tech startup already kept its contract metadata in PostgreSQL on RDS and wanted semantic clause search for its law-firm customers. Instead of adding a separate vector database, they ran `CREATE EXTENSION vector` and added an `embedding vector(1024)` column to the `clauses` table, next to `firm_id`, `contract_id` and a **JSONB** `meta` column with a GIN index for queries like `meta @> '{"type":"indemnity"}'`.

An **HNSW** index with `vector_cosine_ops` and queries ordered by `embedding <=> $1` gave good recall. The key win was isolation: every query had `WHERE firm_id = $2` as an ordinary clause in the same transactional store, so a firm could never see another firm's clauses, and one backup covered everything.

The incident came a month in. Search latency tripled and the `clauses` table had grown to three times its expected size. The embedding backfill job updated rows in batches, and under **MVCC** each update wrote a new tuple and left a **dead tuple** behind. Normally autovacuum would clean them, but an analytics session had held a transaction open for two days, pinning old versions so VACUUM could not remove them. Killing the session and letting autovacuum catch up fixed it; they also set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and made autovacuum more aggressive on that table.

The architect's summary to the client: PostgreSQL won here because vectors, permissions and metadata sit in one place, not because it beats SQL Server everywhere.
inPractice.flow:
query text --embed--> vector(1024)
   SELECT ... FROM clauses
   WHERE firm_id = $2 AND meta @> '{"type":"indemnity"}'   (GIN)
   ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5                      (HNSW)
backfill UPDATEs --> dead tuples --> autovacuum
   blocked by 2-day open transaction --> bloat --> slow search
inPractice.takeaway: PostgreSQL's MVCC never blocks readers, but dead tuples need VACUUM; with pgvector I keep embeddings, metadata and permission filters in one transactional store.

lesson.body:
**Concurrency.** SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED uses locks; RCSI or SNAPSHOT add row versioning kept in a version store. PostgreSQL is MVCC all the way down: an UPDATE writes a new tuple and marks the old one dead, readers never block writers. The cost is bloat. **Autovacuum** reclaims dead tuples and freezes old transaction IDs; if it falls behind on a hot table, the table and its indexes grow and queries slow. A long-open transaction pins old versions so VACUUM cannot remove them, a classic production incident. Also, PostgreSQL tables are heaps: there is no clustered index that keeps rows ordered.

**JSONB** stores parsed binary JSON. A GIN index supports containment queries like `metadata @> '{"matter":"M-42"}'`. SQL Server stores JSON as text with JSON_VALUE and computed-column indexes (SQL Server 2025 adds a native json type), so PostgreSQL is the more natural home for semi-structured data.

**Extensions** are first-class: PostGIS, pg_trgm, pg_stat_statements and **pgvector**. pgvector adds `vector(n)`, operators `<->` (L2), `<=>` (cosine distance) and `<#>` (negative inner product), and approximate indexes **HNSW** (better recall/speed, slower build) or **IVFFlat**. For RAG this means chunks, embeddings, matter ids and permissions live in one transactional store, filtered with plain WHERE clauses; Aurora PostgreSQL can serve as a Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector store.

**When to choose it:** no licence cost, strong on Linux and every cloud, rich types and extensions, vectors next to relational data. Choose SQL Server when the estate, tooling (SSRS, SSIS, Agent), skills and licences are already Microsoft-centric. Small gotchas: identifiers fold to lowercase, `LIMIT` instead of `TOP`, and `ILIKE` for case-insensitive matching.

cards.prompt: A PostgreSQL table with heavy updates keeps growing on disk even though the row count is stable. What is the most likely cause?
options: Autovacuum is not keeping up, or a long-running transaction prevents dead tuples from being removed
The clustered index is fragmented
JSONB columns are compressed badly
The WAL is stored inside the table
cards.why: Every update leaves a dead tuple; if VACUUM cannot reclaim them the table bloats. PostgreSQL has no clustered index, so the SQL Server-style fragmentation answer is the tempting wrong one.

cards.prompt: In PostgreSQL, readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers under the default isolation level.
cards.why: MVCC gives each statement a snapshot of committed versions, so plain SELECTs take no row locks that conflict with UPDATEs. SQL Server needs RCSI or SNAPSHOT to behave this way.

cards.prompt: In pgvector, the operator ___ returns cosine distance between two vectors.
cards.why: <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance, <#> is negative inner product, <=> is cosine distance. The index operator class (vector_cosine_ops) must match the operator or the index is not used.

cards.prompt: Which index type speeds up JSONB containment queries such as meta @> '{"status":"open"}'?
options: GIN
B-tree on the whole column
HNSW
Hash
cards.why: GIN indexes every key and value inside the document, which is what containment needs. A B-tree compares whole values, and HNSW is for vector similarity.

cards.prompt: For a RAG feature where each chunk must be filtered by matter and user permissions before similarity ranking, what is a strong argument for pgvector?
options: Embeddings, metadata and permission data live in one transactional database and filter with ordinary SQL
pgvector is always faster than any dedicated vector engine
PostgreSQL needs no indexes for vectors
It removes the need to chunk documents
cards.why: Keeping vectors beside relational data makes permission filtering and consistency simple. Dedicated engines like OpenSearch may scale better for huge corpora or hybrid keyword search, so 'always faster' is wrong.

cards.prompt: pgvector's ___ index builds a layered proximity graph and usually gives better speed-recall trade-offs than IVFFlat, at the cost of slower builds.
cards.why: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) needs no training step and handles inserts well; IVFFlat clusters vectors into lists and should be built after data is loaded.

explain.prompt: You used both SQL Server and PostgreSQL at Moveo. What is the most important difference under the hood, and when would you choose PostgreSQL?
explain.modelAnswer: The deepest difference is concurrency. SQL Server by default uses locking read committed, so long reads and writes can block each other unless you enable RCSI, which keeps row versions in a version store. PostgreSQL is MVCC by design: an update writes a new row version in the table and leaves the old one dead, readers see a snapshot and never block writers. The trade-off is that VACUUM must clean dead tuples, and long-open transactions or a lagging autovacuum cause bloat. Also, Postgres tables are heaps, there is no clustered index. I would choose PostgreSQL when licence cost and Linux or cloud portability matter, when the data is semi-structured and JSONB with GIN fits, or when I want extensions, especially pgvector to keep RAG embeddings next to metadata and permissions in one transactional store. I would stay with SQL Server when the client's tooling, reporting and team are already Microsoft-centric. Then add your own example: [which Moveo service used Postgres and why].
rubric: Explains MVCC vs locking default correctly
Mentions VACUUM/dead tuples and bloat risk
Notes heap tables / no clustered index
Gives concrete reasons to choose Postgres (cost, JSONB, extensions)
Connects pgvector to RAG with metadata filtering

scenarios.situation: A law firm client wants a first RAG prototype over 200,000 document chunks, each tagged with matter id and access group. They already run PostgreSQL on Amazon RDS for their matter system. Budget is tight and the demo is in three weeks.
scenarios.question: Where do you store the embeddings?

options.text: Add pgvector to a PostgreSQL instance, store chunks with matter and access columns, HNSW index, and filter by permissions in the same query
options.why: Reuses a database they already operate, scales comfortably to this size, and makes permission filtering plain SQL, which matters most for a law firm.

options.text: Stand up Amazon OpenSearch Service for vectors and keep metadata in PostgreSQL
options.why: Valid and better for hybrid keyword search at scale, but adds a second system to sync and secure for a three-week prototype.

options.text: Keep embeddings in a Python list in memory and filter permissions in the UI
options.why: Nothing persists, and filtering permissions in the UI means privileged chunks already reached the model or the client.

nodes.title: MongoDB document modelling
nodes.tease: You embedded every comment in the post. One viral post later, writes fail. What limit hit?

primer.problem: MongoDB lets you store whole objects as documents, which is fast to build with, but a bad shape hurts later: documents grow without limit, updates touch many places, reports need joins MongoDB is weak at. Defending it on your CV means knowing how to model, index and query it, and when to avoid it.
primer.picture: A document is like a C# object graph serialised to JSON (BSON) and stored as one unit. **Embedding** is putting a child list inside the parent object; **referencing** is storing only an id, like a foreign key without enforcement. Rule of thumb: model for how the app reads. Data read together and bounded in size gets embedded; data shared, unbounded or updated independently gets referenced. The **aggregation pipeline** is like chained LINQ operators over a collection.

terms.def: Binary JSON, MongoDB's storage format; adds types like ObjectId, Date and Decimal128 and caps a document at 16 MB.
Storing related data inside the parent document, so one read returns everything and one write is atomic.
Storing another document's _id instead of its contents, resolved by a second query or $lookup.
An ordered list of stages like $match, $group and $lookup that transforms documents step by step.
Compound index ordering guideline: Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields.

inPractice.setting: A parcel-logistics firm tracking 2 million shipments a day across 30 depots
inPractice.story:
A parcel carrier modelled each shipment as one MongoDB document, which was a good start: sender, recipient and the parcel lines are read together and bounded, so **embedding** them made the tracking page one read and every status write atomic. The problem was the `scans` array. Every depot scan, sensor ping and delivery attempt was pushed into it, and international parcels collected thousands of entries.

Saves for those shipments slowed to seconds because each `$push` rewrote a large document, and one pallet of returns that bounced between depots for weeks failed with a document-size error at the 16 MB limit. The team split the model. The shipment kept a **subset** of the latest 10 scans for the tracking page, and the full history moved to a `scan_buckets` collection using the **bucket** pattern, one document per shipment per hour, **referencing** the shipment by `_id`. A **TTL** index expires buckets after 18 months, matching the retention policy.

The depot dashboard was the second fix. `explain('executionStats')` on "open shipments for depot X, newest first, weight over 20 kg" showed a `COLLSCAN` examining 4 million documents to return 50. Following **ESR**, they built `{ depotId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1, weightKg: 1 }`: equality, sort, then range. Documents examined fell to 52.

When finance asked for cross-shipment invoicing with strict invariants, the team kept that in PostgreSQL rather than stretching multi-document transactions across the tracking store.
inPractice.flow:
scanner --> shipments.updateOne($push to latest 10, $slice)
         \-> scan_buckets.updateOne({shipmentId, hour}, upsert)
tracking page --> shipments (one read: parcel + latest scans)
depot dashboard --> shipments index {depotId, status, createdAt, weightKg}
scan_buckets --> TTL index expires after 18 months
inPractice.takeaway: I embed what is bounded and read together, and reference anything that grows without limit; unbounded arrays are the classic MongoDB failure, and ESR guides compound indexes.

lesson.body:
**Embed vs reference.** Embed when the child belongs to the parent, is read with it and stays bounded: an order with its line items, an employee with their addresses. A single-document write is atomic, so embedding also gives you consistency for free. Reference when the child list grows without bound (comments, audit events, log lines), when the data is shared by many parents (a product used in many orders), or when it is updated on its own schedule. Unbounded arrays are the classic mistake: documents cap at **16 MB**, and long before that every update rewrites a big document. Patterns like **subset** (embed the latest 10, reference the rest) and **bucket** (group time series by hour) sit in between.

**Indexes** are B-trees like SQL Server's. Compound index order follows **ESR**: equality, then sort, then range. Indexing an array field creates a **multikey** index. **TTL** indexes expire documents after a time, **partial** indexes cover only matching documents. Use `explain('executionStats')` and look for `COLLSCAN` and the ratio of documents examined to returned.

The **aggregation pipeline** chains stages: put `$match` (and `$sort` on an indexed field) first so indexes are used, then `$group`, `$project`, `$lookup` for joins, `$unwind` for arrays. `$lookup` exists but is not a relational engine; heavy joins hint at the wrong database.

**Transactions**: multi-document ACID transactions exist since 4.0 on replica sets and 4.2 on sharded clusters, with a default 60-second lifetime. They work, but needing them everywhere suggests your model should be relational.

**When not to use it:** strongly relational data with cross-entity invariants and ad-hoc reporting, like payroll or accounting. For an AI stack, MongoDB Atlas adds `$vectorSearch`, but the modelling questions stay the same.

cards.prompt: Which data is the best candidate for embedding inside its parent document?
options: An invoice's line items, always read with the invoice and limited in number
Every audit event ever recorded for a user
Product details shared by thousands of orders
Chat messages in a channel that never closes
cards.why: Bounded, owned and read together is the embedding sweet spot. Audit events and chat messages grow without bound toward the 16 MB cap, and shared product data would need updating in thousands of places.

cards.prompt: A single MongoDB document cannot exceed ___ in size.
cards.why: The BSON document limit is 16 MB. Unbounded embedded arrays hit performance problems long before that, because each update rewrites a growing document.

cards.prompt: A query filters status = 'open', sorts by createdAt and filters total > 100. Which compound index order follows the ESR rule?
options: { status: 1, createdAt: -1, total: 1 }
{ total: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
{ createdAt: -1, total: 1, status: 1 }
{ status: 1, total: 1, createdAt: -1 }
cards.why: Equality first narrows to one contiguous range, sort next lets the index deliver order without an in-memory sort, range last. Putting the range before the sort is the tempting mistake and forces a blocking sort.

cards.prompt: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets and sharded clusters.
cards.why: Since 4.0 on replica sets and 4.2 on sharded clusters. They carry overhead and a default 60-second limit, so a model that needs them on every write is a sign the data is relational.

cards.prompt: Why should $match come as early as possible in an aggregation pipeline?
options: So it can use an index and reduce documents before expensive stages like $group or $lookup
Because $match is not allowed after $group
Because the pipeline runs stages in reverse order
So results are returned sorted
cards.why: An initial $match can use indexes like a find(); later stages work on in-memory documents. $match after $group is allowed (it acts like HAVING), it just cannot use the collection's indexes.

cards.prompt: A payroll system with strict cross-table invariants and frequent ad-hoc finance reports is a natural fit for MongoDB.
cards.why: Payroll is relational: employees, contracts, periods and payslips with constraints and joins, plus ad-hoc reporting. That is SQL Server or PostgreSQL territory, which is why the ERP's payroll stays relational.

explain.prompt: Your CV lists MongoDB at Moveo. What did you store there rather than in SQL Server or PostgreSQL, and how did you decide the document shape?
explain.modelAnswer: Start with your real case: [which service, what kind of data]. The reason to choose MongoDB was that the data was document-shaped: read and written as a whole, with a schema that varies per record, and little need for cross-entity joins or ad-hoc reporting. For the shape I modelled around the access pattern. Things always read with the parent and bounded in size were embedded, so one read serves the screen and one write is atomic. Things that grow without bound or are shared, such as events or history, went into their own collection with a reference, because of the 16 MB limit and because rewriting big documents on each update is slow. Indexes followed the queries using equality, sort, range order, and I checked explain output for collection scans. I would not put payroll or tender approvals there: those need relational constraints and reporting, so they stayed in SQL Server. MongoDB transactions exist, but if I needed them on every write I would take that as a sign the data belongs in a relational store.
rubric: Names a concrete use and why documents fit it
Embed vs reference decided by access pattern and growth
Mentions the 16 MB limit or unbounded arrays
Index design follows queries (ESR, explain)
States when not to use MongoDB

scenarios.situation: A tender module stores each tender as a MongoDB document with an embedded array of every bid revision and every status change. Large tenders now take seconds to save and one write failed with a document-size error.
scenarios.question: How do you fix the model?

options.text: Move bid revisions and status history into separate collections referencing the tender id, keep only current bids and status embedded, and index the history by tenderId and time
options.why: Splits the unbounded parts out while keeping the common read cheap: the subset pattern. History becomes an append-only collection, which is also the right shape for an audit trail.

options.text: Compress the array with a custom serializer
options.why: Delays the size error but every save still rewrites a growing document; the model is still wrong.

options.text: Split each tender across several documents with numbered suffixes when it gets large
options.why: Ad hoc sharding of one entity makes every read and update complex and breaks single-document atomicity, the main reason to embed.

nodes.title: Redis caching
nodes.tease: Redis is full. Your default policy is noeviction. What does the next write get back?

primer.problem: Microservices hit the same database rows again and again: user permissions, lookup lists, session data. Redis keeps hot data in memory so responses are fast and the database breathes. But a cache brings its own questions: what happens when memory fills, when data changes, when Redis restarts, and who owns the licence.
primer.picture: Redis is a networked `Dictionary<string, T>` living in RAM, where T can be a string, hash, list, set, sorted set or stream, each with atomic commands. In **cache-aside**, your service checks Redis first, falls back to SQL on a miss and writes the result with a **TTL**. When memory reaches `maxmemory`, the **eviction policy** decides what gets dropped. **RDB** snapshots and the **AOF** log decide what survives a restart.
primer.sketch:
GET user:42:perms ──hit──▶ return
      │ miss
      ▼
 SELECT ... FROM SQL Server
      │
      ▼
 SET user:42:perms <json> EX 300 ──▶ return

 on update: write SQL, then DEL user:42:perms

terms.def: The application reads the cache first, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result itself.
Time to live: seconds until Redis deletes a key automatically, set with EX on SET or with EXPIRE.
The maxmemory-policy setting that decides which keys Redis removes when memory is full, or whether writes fail instead.
Redis persistence: RDB writes point-in-time snapshots, AOF appends every write command to a log for replay.
A Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD licence, created after Redis changed licence in 2024.
A number that increases with each lock grant, letting the protected resource reject writes from an older lock holder.

inPractice.setting: A card-payments fintech authorising 3,000 transactions a second across 12 microservices
inPractice.story:
Every card authorisation at a payments fintech checked the merchant's risk profile and fee rules in SQL Server, and at peak those lookups were 70% of database load. The team put Redis in front with **cache-aside**: read `merchant:{id}:rules`, on a miss load from SQL and `SET ... EX 300` plus a random 0-60 seconds of jitter so keys did not expire together. When the risk team changed rules, the service wrote SQL and then deleted the key instead of updating it.

The first outage came on Black Friday. Redis hit `maxmemory`, and because the policy was still the default `noeviction`, every write returned an OOM error, which the client library surfaced as failed authorisations. The instance was a pure cache, so they switched to **allkeys-lfu**: traffic was skewed toward a few thousand big merchants, and LFU keeps those hot keys resident.

The second problem was subtler. A nightly settlement job used a lock, `SET lock:settlement token NX PX 30000`, released by a Lua script that checked the token. One night a long GC pause outlived the 30-second expiry, a second instance took the lock, and both started settling. The duplicate ledger rows were rejected only because the ledger table had a unique constraint on the settlement batch. The team added a fencing token checked by the database and stopped treating the Redis lock as the guarantee.

They later moved to Valkey on ElastiCache, sidestepping the licence questions.
inPractice.flow:
auth-service --GET merchant:42:rules--> Redis --hit--> decide
        |miss
        v
   SQL Server --> SET merchant:42:rules <json> EX 300+jitter
risk-admin --> UPDATE SQL --> DEL merchant:42:rules
maxmemory reached --> allkeys-lfu evicts cold merchants
inPractice.takeaway: For a cache I set an eviction policy like allkeys-lfu instead of noeviction, delete keys on write, and never trust a Redis lock alone for correctness.

lesson.body:
**Data structures** are the point of Redis: hashes for objects, sorted sets for leaderboards and rate windows, lists and streams for queues, sets for membership, plus HyperLogLog and bitmaps. Redis 8 also folds JSON, the query engine and vector sets into the core.

**Cache-aside**: read Redis, on a miss load from the database and `SET key value EX 300`. On writes, update the database then **delete** the key rather than updating it, which avoids races leaving stale data. Add TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, and protect hot keys from a **stampede** with a short lock or early refresh.

**Eviction**: the default `maxmemory-policy` is `noeviction`, so a full Redis returns OOM errors on writes. For a pure cache use `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu` (LFU keeps frequently used keys, better for skewed traffic). `volatile-*` policies only evict keys that have a TTL, useful when the same instance also holds keys that must not vanish. LRU is approximated by sampling keys, not a perfect list.

**Persistence**: RDB forks and writes a compact snapshot, fast restarts but you lose writes since the last one. AOF logs every write; with `appendfsync everysec` you lose at most about a second. Many run both, or neither for a pure cache.

**Locks**: `SET lock:job token NX PX 30000`, release with a Lua script that deletes only if the token matches. Caveat: a GC pause longer than the expiry lets two holders run; Redlock does not fix that. Use fencing tokens, or let the database enforce correctness.

**Licence**: BSD until March 2024, then RSALv2/SSPLv1 from 7.4, which is not open source. The Linux Foundation forked **Valkey** from 7.2.4 under BSD, backed by AWS and Google. In May 2025 Redis 8 added **AGPLv3** as a third option. AWS ElastiCache and MemoryDB now offer Valkey.
lesson.snippet:
# cache-aside read
GET user:42:perms                 # (nil) -> miss
SET user:42:perms '{"roles":["hr"]}' EX 300

# invalidate after a DB write
DEL user:42:perms

# pure cache: evict any key, least frequently used
CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb
CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu

# lock with owner token and expiry
SET lock:payroll-run 9f2c NX PX 30000
# release only if we still own it (Lua)
EVAL "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:payroll-run 9f2c

cards.prompt: Redis is used purely as a cache and hits maxmemory. Which eviction policy fits best?
options: allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
noeviction
volatile-ttl with no TTLs set
Disable maxmemory
cards.why: For a pure cache any key may go, so evict the least recently or least frequently used. noeviction (the default) makes writes fail with OOM, and volatile-* policies evict nothing if keys have no TTL.

cards.prompt: Redis's default maxmemory-policy is ___, which returns errors on writes when memory is full.
cards.why: The default protects data that must not vanish but surprises teams using Redis as a cache. Setting maxmemory and an eviction policy is a deliberate decision you should be able to defend.

cards.prompt: In cache-aside, after updating a row in SQL Server, what should the service usually do with the cached copy?
options: Delete the key so the next read reloads fresh data
Leave it until the TTL expires
Update the cache first, then the database
Flush the whole Redis database
cards.why: Deleting after the DB write is simple and avoids races where two writers leave an older value cached. Waiting for TTL serves stale data, and updating the cache before the DB can cache a value that then fails to commit.

cards.prompt: With AOF and appendfsync everysec, a crash can lose roughly the last second of writes.
cards.why: Redis fsyncs the log once per second, the usual balance between durability and throughput. RDB-only can lose everything since the last snapshot, possibly minutes.

cards.prompt: Which statement about Redis licensing is correct as of 2026?
options: Redis 8 is available under AGPLv3 alongside RSALv2 and SSPLv1; Valkey is a BSD-licensed fork of 7.2.4
Redis has always been BSD licensed
Redis 7.4 onward is Apache 2.0
Valkey is owned by Redis Ltd.
cards.why: Redis moved from BSD to RSALv2/SSPLv1 in March 2024, which triggered the Linux Foundation's Valkey fork; in May 2025 Redis 8 added AGPLv3 as an open-source option.

cards.prompt: Because a lock holder can pause past its lock's expiry, a safe design passes a ___ to the protected resource so stale holders are rejected.
cards.why: Expiry-based locks cannot guarantee mutual exclusion across GC pauses or network delays. A monotonically increasing token lets the database refuse writes from an older holder.

explain.prompt: You list Redis. What did you cache, what is your eviction policy and why, and what happens when the cached data changes?
explain.modelAnswer: Name your real case: [what you cached at Moveo, e.g. lookups, permissions or sessions, and roughly how hot]. The pattern was cache-aside: the service reads Redis, on a miss loads from SQL Server or Postgres and stores the result with a TTL, with some jitter so keys do not all expire together. When data changes, the service writes the database first and then deletes the key, so the next read repopulates; I prefer delete over update because it avoids races. For eviction: Redis defaults to noeviction, which makes writes fail when memory is full. For a pure cache I set maxmemory and allkeys-lru, or allkeys-lfu when a few keys dominate traffic. If the same instance held data that must not disappear, I would use volatile-lru so only TTL keys are evicted, or better, separate instances. Persistence for a cache can be off or RDB only; if Redis holds sessions I would add AOF with everysec. And for anything correctness-critical, the database stays the source of truth.
rubric: Describes cache-aside with TTL
Invalidation: write DB then delete key, with reasoning
Knows default is noeviction and picks a policy with a reason
Distinguishes allkeys vs volatile policies
Mentions persistence choice matching the use

scenarios.situation: Two instances of the payroll service run a nightly payroll calculation, and you must ensure only one runs it. A teammate proposes a Redis lock with SET NX PX 60000. Runs sometimes take 3 minutes.
scenarios.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: Use the lock only as a first filter, and enforce exclusivity in the database too (a unique run-per-period row or fencing token), so a second runner cannot commit results
options.why: Expiry-based locks can be held by two processes after a pause or a long run; making the database reject duplicates gives real correctness for payroll.

options.text: Raise the expiry to 10 minutes and keep the Redis lock as the only guard
options.why: Reduces the risk for current run times but any slow run or pause beyond 10 minutes still allows double execution.

options.text: Use SET NX without an expiry so the lock never times out
options.why: If the holder crashes, the lock is never released and payroll silently never runs again until someone deletes the key.

nodes.title: Elasticsearch to OpenSearch
nodes.tease: Your CV says Elasticsearch. Their stack says OpenSearch. Same thing, or a trap?

primer.problem: Users want to type a few words and find the right record across millions, ranked by relevance and tolerant of word forms, which a SQL LIKE cannot do. The target role at ISA uses OpenSearch for retrieval in RAG over legal documents, so your Elasticsearch experience must transfer cleanly and you must know where the two differ.
primer.picture: An **inverted index** is the index at the back of a book: each term points to the documents containing it. An **analyzer** decides what counts as a term (lowercase, split, stem). **BM25** scores matches. An index is split into **shards** spread across nodes, each with **replicas**. Vectors add a second index type: **kNN** finds documents whose embeddings are nearest the query's. **Hybrid search** merges both rankings. OpenSearch is the Apache-licensed fork of Elasticsearch 7.10.2 with the same core.

terms.def: A map from each term to the list of documents and positions where it appears, the core of full-text search.
Character filters, a tokenizer and token filters that turn text into the terms stored and searched.
The default relevance formula: rewards rare terms and repeated matches, with diminishing returns and document-length normalisation.
A self-contained Lucene index holding part of an Elasticsearch or OpenSearch index; primaries are fixed at creation.
The schema of an index: each field's type, such as text, keyword, date or vector, and its analyzer.
Combining keyword (BM25) and vector (kNN) results into one ranking, for example with reciprocal rank fusion.

inPractice.setting: A news publisher's 6-million-article archive moving from Elasticsearch 7.10 to OpenSearch
inPractice.story:
A national news publisher ran its archive search on self-managed Elasticsearch 7.10. Editors searched 6 million articles by headline and body, and a `keyword` subfield on `byline.raw` drove author filters and aggregations. When the licence change made legal nervous, the team moved to Amazon OpenSearch Service; because OpenSearch forked from 7.10.2, the Query DSL and most mappings carried over unchanged.

The migration was also the chance to fix an old mistake. Dynamic mapping had created thousands of fields from embedded widget metadata, and the `body` field used the standard analyzer, so 'elections' did not match 'election'. A field's type or analyzer cannot be changed in place, so they created `articles-v2` with an explicit **mapping** and the `english` analyzer, ran `_reindex`, and flipped the `articles` **alias** in one call. The app never noticed.

Then the newsroom asked for an AI research assistant that answers questions over the archive. The first version used pure **kNN** on a `knn_vector` field, and it failed on exactly what journalists search most: a politician's name or a bill number like 'HB 2471' came back as vaguely related articles. Embeddings capture meaning, not exact tokens. The team switched to **hybrid search**: a `hybrid` query combining a BM25 `match` with the kNN clause, through a search pipeline that normalises and combines the two scores. Exact names now rank first, and paraphrased questions still find the right stories.
inPractice.flow:
question --embed--> vector
   GET articles/_search?search_pipeline=hybrid-norm
      hybrid: [ match(body, english analyzer) -> BM25 scores
                knn(embedding, k=20)          -> vector scores ]
      pipeline: normalise + combine --> top passages --> LLM
alias articles --> articles-v2 (after _reindex)
inPractice.takeaway: Pure vector search misses exact names and identifiers; I use OpenSearch hybrid search, combining BM25 and kNN through a normalisation pipeline, and reindex behind an alias for mapping changes.

lesson.body:
**Inverted index and analyzers.** At index time a `text` field runs through an analyzer: the standard analyzer tokenises on word boundaries and lowercases; language analyzers add stemming and stop words. The same analyzer runs on the query, so 'Contracts' matches 'contract'. A `keyword` field is stored as one exact term, used for filters, sorting and aggregations. A common mapping is both: `title` as text with a `title.raw` keyword subfield.

**Mappings** should be explicit; dynamic mapping guesses types and can explode field counts. You cannot change an existing field's type: create a new index and `_reindex`, with an **alias** so the switch is invisible to the app.

**BM25** is the default similarity: term frequency with saturation (k1 = 1.2), inverse document frequency, and length normalisation (b = 0.75).

**Shards and replicas.** Primary shard count is fixed at creation (split or shrink aside); replicas can change any time and are never placed on the same node as their primary. Avoid many tiny shards. Search is near real time: new documents become visible after a refresh, every second by default.

**Vectors.** Elasticsearch uses `dense_vector` with an HNSW index and the `knn` search option; hybrid ranking uses the RRF retriever. OpenSearch uses `knn_vector` from its k-NN plugin, engines Faiss or Lucene, and hybrid search via the `hybrid` query plus a search pipeline that normalises and combines scores.

**The fork.** In 2021 Elastic moved from Apache 2.0 to SSPL and the Elastic License; AWS forked 7.10.2 as **OpenSearch** (Apache 2.0). Since 2024 it is governed by the OpenSearch Software Foundation under the Linux Foundation, and OpenSearch 3.0 (2025) moved to Lucene 10. Elastic added AGPLv3 in 2024. Query DSL is largely shared; clients, built-in security, Dashboards versus Kibana and vector APIs differ. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is a common vector store for Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

cards.prompt: You need to filter by exact matter number and also aggregate by it. How should matter_id be mapped?
options: keyword
text with the standard analyzer
text with the english analyzer
dense_vector
cards.why: keyword stores the value as one exact term, which filters, sorts and aggregates correctly. A text field would be tokenised, so 'M-2026-0418' could split into pieces and match the wrong matters.

cards.prompt: You can increase the number of replica shards of an existing index at any time, but not freely change its number of primary shards.
cards.why: Replicas are copies and can be added or removed live. Primaries define how documents are routed, so changing them needs split/shrink or a reindex into a new index.

cards.prompt: Why was OpenSearch created?
options: Elastic moved Elasticsearch from Apache 2.0 to SSPL and the Elastic License in 2021, so AWS forked version 7.10.2 under Apache 2.0
Elasticsearch could not run on AWS
To add vector search, which Elasticsearch never supported
Elastic sold Elasticsearch to Amazon
cards.why: The 2021 licence change is the origin. Both now support vector search; OpenSearch is governed by the OpenSearch Software Foundation under the Linux Foundation since 2024.

cards.prompt: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch rank full-text matches by default with the ___ similarity algorithm.
cards.why: BM25 replaced classic TF-IDF as the default in Elasticsearch 5.0 and OpenSearch inherited it; it saturates term frequency and normalises for document length.

cards.prompt: In RAG over legal documents, why combine BM25 with vector kNN search?
options: Vectors capture meaning while BM25 catches exact terms like clause numbers, party names and case citations that embeddings blur
BM25 is needed to compute embeddings
kNN cannot return more than one result
Hybrid search removes the need for permission filters
cards.why: Embeddings are good at paraphrase but weak on rare exact tokens; lawyers search for exactly those. Hybrid search still needs permission filters, so the last option is a dangerous misconception.

cards.prompt: To change a field's type without downtime, create a new index with the new mapping, reindex, and switch an ___ to point at it.
cards.why: The application queries the alias, so the cut-over is atomic. Field types cannot be changed in place because existing segments were built with the old type.

explain.prompt: You used Elasticsearch at Moveo. We use OpenSearch. Explain how full-text search works under the hood, and what changes for you moving to OpenSearch.
explain.modelAnswer: Under the hood both are Lucene. At index time each text field runs through an analyzer, character filters, a tokenizer and token filters such as lowercase and stemming, and the resulting terms go into an inverted index, a map from term to the documents containing it. Queries run through the same analyzer, look up postings lists and score with BM25, which rewards rare terms and repeated matches but normalises for document length. Keyword fields store exact values for filters and aggregations. An index is split into primary shards fixed at creation plus replicas for availability and read throughput. Then your case: [what you indexed at Moveo and why]. Moving to OpenSearch: it is the Apache-licensed fork of Elasticsearch 7.10.2 from 2021, now under the Linux Foundation, so mappings, analyzers and most query DSL transfer. The differences are the clients, security as a built-in plugin, Dashboards instead of Kibana, and vectors: knn_vector with Faiss or Lucene engines and hybrid search through a normalisation search pipeline, which is what RAG retrieval at ISA would use.
rubric: Explains analyzer to inverted index to BM25 correctly
Distinguishes text vs keyword
Explains shards and replicas
Knows OpenSearch is the 2021 fork of 7.10.2 and why
Names concrete differences, especially knn_vector and hybrid search

explain.prompt: How would you design retrieval in OpenSearch for a RAG assistant over a law firm's documents?
explain.modelAnswer: One index of chunks, each with the text, a knn_vector embedding, and keyword metadata: matter id, document id, access groups, privilege flag, dates. Explicit mappings, an English analyzer on the body and an alias so I can reindex when the chunking or embedding model changes. Retrieval is hybrid: a BM25 match on the body, because lawyers search for exact clause numbers, names and citations, plus a kNN query on the embedding, combined through a search pipeline that normalises and merges scores, or reciprocal rank fusion. Permission filters on matter and access group are applied inside the query, as filters on both sub-queries, never after retrieval, so privileged chunks never reach the model. I would log each query with the returned chunk ids and scores for the audit trail, and evaluate recall on a labelled question set before tuning k, chunk size or weights.
rubric: Chunk index with vector plus keyword metadata
Hybrid BM25 + kNN with a stated fusion method
Permission filtering inside the query, not after
Alias/reindex plan for model or chunking changes
Logging for audit and an evaluation set

scenarios.situation: A law firm's RAG prototype on OpenSearch uses pure vector kNN. Associates complain that searching for 'clause 14.2(b)' or a specific party name returns loosely related passages instead of the exact clause.
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.text: Add a BM25 match on the text field and combine it with kNN via a hybrid query and normalisation pipeline, then measure on a set of real associate queries
options.why: Exact tokens are BM25's strength and embeddings' weakness; hybrid search fixes both query types, and an evaluation set proves it.

options.text: Switch to a larger embedding model
options.why: May help a little, but embeddings still blur exact identifiers like clause numbers, and it costs a full re-embed.

options.text: Increase k from 10 to 200 and let the LLM find the right clause
options.why: Floods the context with noise, raises cost and latency, and still may not retrieve the exact clause.

questions.prompt: A report query that took 2 seconds now takes 40 seconds after a large data load. Nothing was deployed. Walk me through diagnosing and fixing it.
questions.modelOutline: Reproduce with the real parameters and capture the actual execution plan with STATISTICS IO and TIME, so there is a baseline. Check Query Store: did the plan change after the load? Compare estimated and actual rows on the expensive operators; a large gap after a load usually means stale statistics, since auto-update thresholds may not have fired, or a plan sniffed for an unrepresentative parameter. Update statistics on the loaded tables and re-test. If the plan is still poor, look for scans caused by non-SARGable predicates or implicit conversions, and key lookups that grew with the data; fix with a covering index or rewrite. For sniffing, use OPTION RECOMPILE for the report or force the known-good plan in Query Store. Also rule out blocking from the load itself, which RCSI avoids for readers. Verify with before and after numbers and add a post-load statistics step so it does not recur.
rubric: Reproduces with real parameters and captures the actual plan
Uses Query Store or plan history to see if the plan changed
Compares estimated vs actual rows
Identifies stale statistics after the load and updates them
Checks SARGability, implicit conversions, key lookups
Knows parameter sniffing fixes (RECOMPILE, forced plan)
Rules out blocking from the load
Verifies and prevents recurrence (post-load stats job)

questions.prompt: Your CV lists SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch. For a RAG assistant over a law firm's documents with a full audit trail, which of these would you use, for what, and why not the others?
questions.modelOutline: Map each store to a job. Relational system of record (SQL Server or PostgreSQL) for matters, users, permissions and the audit trail, append-only with request id, user, retrieved chunk ids and model id. Retrieval in OpenSearch, the Apache-licensed fork of Elasticsearch, with hybrid BM25 plus kNN because lawyers search exact clauses and names, and permission filters inside the query. Alternatively pgvector in PostgreSQL for a smaller corpus, keeping vectors next to permissions in one transactional store. Redis only as a cache for permissions or embeddings of frequent queries, never as the source of truth, with a clear eviction policy and short TTLs so revoked access does not linger. MongoDB is not needed unless document metadata is truly schemaless; the relational store and the search index cover it. Close with operational cost: fewer systems to secure in a regulated client is a feature.
rubric: Assigns a relational store as system of record for permissions and audit
Picks OpenSearch or pgvector for retrieval with reasons
Hybrid search justified by exact legal terms
Permission filtering inside retrieval
Redis only as cache, with TTL concern for revoked access
Justifies leaving MongoDB out (or a narrow role)
Mentions audit trail contents
Weighs operational and security cost of more systems
